claim: Across 351 web-based gig platforms, only 8.6 percent of 163 million registered user accounts were estimated to be active, implying that roughly 91 percent of people who sign up to earn on a platform never meaningfully work on it.
stance_target: The position that platform-mediated income work has extreme silent attrition, with the overwhelming majority of entrants producing no output
scope_conditions: Global; web-based online gig platforms (freelancing and microtask), NOT content-creation platforms; estimate published 2021 by Kassi, Lehdonvirta and Stephany, reproduced in the World Bank 2023 report; machine-learning database mapping of 351 platforms, not a worker survey
quoted_support: 163 million registered users, of which on average only 8.6 percent (14 million) are active
time_period: 2021 estimate, published in the 2023 World Bank report

claim: On a sample of gig platforms, about one-third of registered workers completed at least one project successfully, but 10 percent or fewer ever completed ten projects or earned more than US$1,000 on the platform.
stance_target: The position that reaching any meaningful cumulative income threshold is achieved by only a small single-digit-to-low-double-digit minority of people who start
scope_conditions: Global; online gig platforms; Pesole and Rani (ILO/JRC), cited as forthcoming as of the 2023 World Bank report; sample size of platforms not disclosed in the citing text; freelancing/microtask work, not content creation
quoted_support: in a sample of given platforms, about one-third of registered workers have completed at least one project successfully, while only 10 percent or fewer have completed 10 projects or earned more than US$1,000 on the platforms.

claim: The World Bank's own web-traffic model contradicts the widely-cited 8.6 percent active-worker figure by more than fourfold, estimating a mean active share of 37 percent and a median of 26 percent across 503 platforms.
stance_target: The position that the 8.6 percent active-share figure is a settled measurement of platform attrition
scope_conditions: Global; n = 503 online gig platforms with available traffic data; 2023; 'active' proxied by monthly unique visitors x (1 - bounce rate) x a 0.755 worker-to-client ratio, divided by registered users adjusted by 1.834 for multihoming and 1.19 for multiworking; the report itself states platforms do not publish active counts and use inconsistent definitions of 'active'
quoted_support: The average proportion of active workers out of registered workers is 37 percent, with a median of 26 percent. This is higher than findings in prior studies that found active-worker shares of 8.6 percent (Kassi, Lehdonvirta, and Stephany 2021), 10 percent (Kuek et al. 2015), and 33 percent (one-project threshold) or 10 percent (10-project threshold)

claim: The distribution of active-worker share across platforms is bimodal rather than uniformly low: 174 of 503 platforms sat in the 0-20 percent active band while 180 sat in the 80-100 percent band, so any single headline attrition rate conceals two structurally different platform types.
stance_target: The assumption that a single global attrition percentage describes creator or gig-worker survival
scope_conditions: Global; n = 503 gig platforms with traffic data; 2023; the report attributes the high-active cluster to curated/vetted-pool business models or to traffic overestimation
quoted_support: in most cases, only a small fraction (0 to 10 percent) of workers actively engage on the platform, but there is a sizeable percentage (35 percent) of platforms with a large share of active workers (over 81 percent).
numbers: 35 percent of platforms over 81 percent active

claim: Only about one in three online gig workers does the work as a main occupation, with two-thirds treating it as secondary or sporadic, so headline worker counts overstate the number of people for whom platform income is an occupation.
stance_target: The position that platform income work is overwhelmingly supplementary rather than a primary occupation
scope_conditions: 17 countries including the Philippines, Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Indonesia; RIWI river-sampling online survey run by the World Bank study team, with 956 online-gig-worker responses within the larger sample; 2021-2023; gig work, not content creation
quoted_support: The team's global survey in 17 countries found that one in three gig workers does online work as their main occupation, while for two-thirds it is a secondary occupation or is performed only sporadically

claim: The World Bank's model-based estimates of online gig workers were validated against the Vietnam 2021 Labour Force Survey and were 20 percent higher than the LFS for Vietnam and 6 percent lower than the LFS-based estimate for the Philippines for main gig workers, but more than four times higher once secondary and marginal workers were included.
stance_target: The reliability of modelled platform-worker counts in Southeast Asia relative to national statistical office data
scope_conditions: Vietnam and Philippines; Vietnam 2021 Labour Force Survey used as ground truth, with Philippines estimated by applying Vietnamese occupation-industry shares; 2021-2023; only self-employed internet-using respondents in gig-similar occupations were counted
quoted_support: For the main gig workers, our estimates are 6 percent lower than the LFS-based estimation for the Philippines and close to 20 percent higher than that for Vietnam. If we focus on the main, secondary, and tertiary gig workers, our estimates are more than four times higher than what the LFS-based results suggest.

claim: Demand for online gig labour is overwhelmingly Western while supply is not: high-income countries generate 77.2 percent of global demand (US alone 36.83 percent) whereas the Philippines generates only 1.00 percent, so Southeast Asian platform earners depend structurally on Western buyers.
stance_target: The position that Southeast Asian platform income is exposed to Western demand conditions and cannot be modelled from domestic market size
scope_conditions: Global, 2022 reference year; demand measured by job postings on online gig platforms; freelancing marketplaces, not content platforms
quoted_support: More than three-quarters of the global demand comes from high-income countries, but the demand from developing countries is rising faster than that in the developed countries

claim: Self-reported platform earnings in the World Bank study are subject to acknowledged upward bias and mid-survey dropout that is concentrated exactly among the population of interest, making self-reported gig and creator income figures systematically optimistic.
stance_target: The position that survivorship and self-report bias inflate all self-reported creator and gig income figures
scope_conditions: Global online survey (RIWI river sampling), 17 countries, 2021-2023; caveat stated by the authors about their own data
quoted_support: We found that individuals who identified as online gig workers and high school graduates were most likely to drop out before finishing the survey.

claim: In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, 41 percent of online gig workers earned under US$200 per month compared with over 90 percent of informal workers, showing that platform work raises the earnings floor without lifting most workers to a living wage.
stance_target: The position that platform income in developing countries beats the informal-sector alternative but still leaves a large minority below subsistence thresholds
scope_conditions: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, Pakistan; World Bank study-team survey compared against the Pakistan Labour Force Survey 2020; pooled regression controlling for age, education and marital status; gig work, not content creation; South Asia not Southeast Asia
quoted_support: Over 90 percent of the informal workers earn less than US$200 per month, while the same parameter is only 41 percent for online gig workers

claim: Global estimates of the gig workforce span a factor of nearly three (154 million to 435 million, or 4.4 to 12.5 percent of the global labour force) depending on method, so no precise population denominator exists against which creator or gig attrition can be computed.
stance_target: The reliability of any denominator used to compute platform-worker or creator survival rates
scope_conditions: Global; 2023; data-science web-traffic method gives the lower bound (excludes mainland China), global survey method gives the upper bound
quoted_support: we estimate that there are between 154 million and 435 million gig workers globally, which means that the share of online gig workers in the global labor force ranges between 4.4 and 12.5 percent.

claim: Content creation is a minority task category within platform gig work, accounting for 19 percent of workers on Malaysia's eRezeki platform versus 54 percent for websites/IT/software, so gig-platform aggregates cannot be read as creator-economy data.
stance_target: The conflation of platform gig-work populations with content-creator populations
scope_conditions: Malaysia; eRezeki platform administrative data supplied by the Malaysia Digital Economy Corporation, 2016-2020; task-category shares among all workers
quoted_support: Sales and Marketing, Social Media, SEO / Writing and Content Creation / Websites, IT and Software / Design, Media and Architecture / Data entry, Admin and Virtual Assistant

claim: The gender pay gap among online gig workers is smaller than in the surrounding national labour market, with women on Workana earning 68 percent of men's earnings in Argentina versus 62 percent economy-wide.
stance_target: The position that platform work compresses but does not eliminate gendered earnings gaps
scope_conditions: Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Mexico; Workana platform survey compared with the latest national labour force surveys, conducted with an Inter-American Development Bank team; earnings measured INDIRECTLY via reservation wage, not observed pay; Latin America, not Southeast Asia
quoted_support: The earnings of online workers in the Workana survey are indirectly inferred by asking them, "What is the minimum monthly salary that a full-time salaried job would have to offer for you to stop doing freelance work on Workana (in USD)?"
